Excellencies, distinguished colleagues, the organizational meeting of the 58th session of the Human Rights Council is now called to order. This meeting is organised in keeping with article 8b of the rules of the Council. We will review the programme of work and share information on the draft resolutions and other initiatives planned during the 58th session. Let us start with the draft programme. The 58th session of the Council will be held from 24 February to 4 April 2025. The latest version of the programme of work is available on the Human Rights Commission intranet. It is an evoluting document that is regularly updated. The draft programme of work indicates that the session will last six weeks. That is because of the rise in mandatory activities, the restrictions that have been imposed on meetings during lunchtime and the official holiday that happens during the session. To ensure completion of work in the time frame, a collective effort will be needed. I thank all of you in advance for your commitment to keeping to speaking times. I also encourage the main authors of resolutions to explore alternative approaches that could allow implementation of their goals while reducing the work of the Council. Signing up online for states on speaking lists for all of the general debates, interactive dialogues and discussions will open on Monday 17th February at 4 p.m. Online inscription, once it is closed, Delegations can still sign up or withdraw by contacting the secretariat in room 20 or by sending an e-mail to the address on the screen. The list of speakers will be closed approximately 15 minutes after each debate starts. I call on all delegations to respect the time frame, by courtesy towards other speakers and the secretariat. Online inscription on the speakers list for the adoption of the EPR results will open on Monday 10th March at 9am and close on Thursday 13th March at 6 o'clock and it will not be possible to sign up after that is closed. For National Human Rights Institutions and NGOs, online sign up for the speakers list for all debates during the session will be available starting from Tuesday 18th February at 2 p.m. Signing up on the speakers list for discussions will be identical to previous sessions. Interested States are invited to classify the discussions by order of preference, and time frames will be granted by the system dependent on preference. If the number of states giving highest priority to a particular discussion goes beyond the maximum possible speaking time, slots will be granted on the principle of first come, first served. Speaking time for discussions is now limited to one minute and 30 seconds. The opening meeting of the session will take place on 24 February at 9 a.m. We will hear statements by the President of the General Assembly, the United Nations Secretary-General, the High Commissioner for Human Rights, and the head of the Federal Department of Foreign Affairs of Switzerland as host country representative. That meeting will be followed by the high-level segment. The Secretary has informed me that to date 104 dignitaries have signed up to participate in the high-level segment. The provisional list of dignitaries is available on the extranet and regularly updated. The speaking time is seven minutes for heads of state and government and five minutes for all other participants within the high-level segment. The high-level segment is reserved to Heads of State, Heads of Government, Deputy Heads of State, Deputy Heads of Government, Ministers, Vice-Ministers, and Heads of specialized institutions, programs, and international organizations. After the high-level segment concludes on Wednesday, 26 February, we will pass immediately to the general segment. during which delegations that were not represented by a dignitary during the high-level segment can take the floor. For the general segment, the speaking time will be limited to three minutes for Member States of the Council and two minutes for observer States and other observers. I draw your attention to the fact that additional security measures may be applied during the high-level segment. Given the large number of participants anticipated on the opening day, the secretariat will communicate relevant information if required. Excellencies, distinguished colleagues, during the 58th session, the Council will hold nine discussions. I now invite the main authors to present their respective initiatives. Delegations that wish to share information on draft resolutions and other initiatives will be able to do so subsequently. The discussions are the following. The first is the high level debate on systematic incorporation of human rights in keeping with resolution 1621 and 574 of the Council. with the topic 30th anniversary of the Beijing Declaration and Programme of Action. The debate will be accessible to persons with disabilities. In keeping with the mandate of this Council to promote effective coordination and mainstreaming of human rights within the United Nations system, this high-level roundtable will bring together United Nations representatives and those of States and other stakeholders to review progress made over the past 30 years in implementing the Beijing declaration and programme of action and to discuss its relevance in addressing the persisting and new challenges, as well as accelerating progress towards equality between women and men. The biennial high-level discussion on the death penalty held in keeping with resolutions 26/2 and 54/35 of the Council, on the topic: "The contribution of the judiciary to promoting human rights and the issue of the death penalty". The debate will be accessible to persons with disabilities. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Belgium to present this initiative on behalf of the main sponsors. You have the floor.

Thank you, President. On the question of death penalty, Belgium would like to brief the Council on the preparations for the biennial high-level panel on the question of the death penalty. That will take place on Tuesday, the 25th of February, from 10 a.m. to 12 p.m. in room 20. As requested by resolution 54/35, this panel discussion will address the contribution of the judiciary to the advancement of human rights and the question of the death penalty. In particular, the panel discussion aims to, first, provide concrete examples of how judiciaries have contributed to the abolition of the death penalty. Second, explore how judiciaries can contribute to a reduction in the application of the death penalty as initial steps towards abolition. Third, discuss how the Council and its mechanisms can support Member States to abide by their international human rights obligations regarding the death penalty. After an opening statement by the High Commissioner for Human Rights, the following speakers will make an intervention. Her Excellency, Ms. Virginia Mabiza, Attorney General of Zimbabwe. Mr. Hicham El Mellati, Director of Criminal Affairs, Pardons, and Crime Detection at the Ministry of Justice of Morocco. The Honorable Mr. Ramkarpal Singh, Member of Parliament and former Deputy Minister in the Prime Minister's Department of Malaysia. and Mr. Donald Patrick Malloy, Chancellor of the University of Maine System and former Governor of the State of Connecticut, United States of America. We believe that the high-level panel will strengthen our understanding of this important issue and provide a useful dialogue that will contribute to the work of this Council and its members. like to encourage everyone's presence and active participation during the interactive dialogue while confining their intervention to the topic of the panel. I thank you, Mr. President.

I thank you. The panel on the implementation of human rights in continuing and strengthening progress made in response to HIV and the need to leave no one behind to be held in resolution 56/20 of the Council will be accessible to persons with disabilities and they get the floor to the distinguished representative of Brazil to present the initiative.

Thank you Mr. President. The panel discussion on the realization of human rights in sustaining and increasing the gains made in the HIV response aims to highlight achievements, challenges, and necessary actions to ensure that no one is left behind in global HIV policies. Convened under the mandate of the Human Rights Council Resolution 56/20, the event will provide the platform for discussing best practices, innovations, and partnerships essential for equitable and sustainable HIV responses. The panel will also examine barriers to access, particularly for key populations, women, and girls, while promoting measures to combat stigma, discrimination, and human rights violations associated with HIV. Panelists from international organizations, academia, and civil society will share their insights, reinforcing the importance of inclusive policies and robust funding mechanisms to advance global commitments. The discussion will also contribute to a forthcoming report by the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights on sustainable HIV response strategies to be presented at the 60th session of the Human Rights Council. The panel will explore ways to integrate HIV services into broader health and social protection systems, emphasizing the importance of enabling laws, policies, and education campaigns. Furthermore, it will address issues on investment gaps and the role of international cooperation in expanding access to treatments, medicines, and technologies necessary for combating HIV. The panel format will include presentations from panelists and we will allow time for interactive discussion and questions. We call for active participation by all delegations and stakeholders, including through joint statements to ensure that viewpoints can be gathered comprehensively and efficiently within the available timeframe on this item. By ensuring accessibility and participation from diverse stakeholders, including persons with disabilities, the panel will reaffirm the Human Rights Council commitment to advancing a rights-based approach to the HIV response, while promoting shared responsibility and global solidarity in achieving the 2025 and 2030 targets. Thank you.

Thank you. That brings us to the panel on early alert, rapid alert and responsibility and prevention of genocides to be held under resolution 5513 of the Council, accessible to persons with disabilities, and I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Armenia to present the initiative. You have the floor.

Thank you. I present the panel on early warning and prevention of genocide, which, as you mentioned, will be held on the 5th of March under resolution 5513. The discussion will be a platform to explore international tools for early warning and prevention of genocide, emphasizing collective efforts to strengthen prevention and response mechanisms. and warning signs, looking at international legal instruments, responsibility and combating impunity. The panel will also be a platform to share good practice and progress made in early warning and prevention, and address the challenges facing States in implementing their commitments and the role of OHCH are working with the Special Council for the Prevention of Genocide to identify the most effective ways to help states to meet their obligations in terms of prevention. We will have a high-level panel of experts to enrich our exchange with recommendations, including Virginia Gamba, special adviser of the Secretary-General for the prevention of genocide, speaking by video message. and also followed by Mublaqar, Special Counsel of the Secretary General for Responsibility for Protection, Mr. Juan Mendez, a human rights specialist and former Special Advisor to the Secretary General on Preventive Genocide, Sean Meschey, Professor in International Law at the George Washington University and former Special Rapporteur on Crimes Against Humanity, And Salita Panday, Executive Center of the Global Center for the Responsibility to Protect. Jo Globa, President of the Human Rights Council, will preside over the panel. In keeping with Resolution 5513, A report of the panel will be prepared by OHCHR and presented at the 59th session of the Council, before the interactive dialogue planned at the 62nd session. We encourage active participation by delegations to enrich the discussion and strengthen our collective commitment to prevent genocide. Thank you.

Thank you. the Panel on the Implementation of the Right to Work and the Right to Social Security in the Informal Sector to be held under resolution 55/9 of the Council. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Egypt to present this initiative on behalf of the main sponsors.

Mr. President, Egypt, on behalf of a cross-regional group comprised of Greece, Indonesia and Romania, is honored to present the panel discussion scheduled on the 7th of March 2025, mandated by the resolution 55/9 that decided to organize during the 58th session. A panel discussion on the realization of the rights to work and to social security in the informal economy. in the context of sustainable and inclusive economies, with an emphasis on the importance of international cooperation and partnerships in this regard. The core group has been presenting the resolution since 2015. The past iterations of the resolution focused on a wide spectrum of themes and issues that are intertwined with the right to work, such as the right to work for women, persons with disabilities, youth, and also the impact of climate change. The upcoming panel discussion shall facilitate discussion on the challenges faced by workers in the informal economy. It will aim at exploring ways to improve their access to decent job opportunities and decent working conditions to expand the social security and to formalize the informal economy. The panel shall also discuss effective ways for the workers in the informal economy to have their concerns heard and to be and to meaningfully participate in the development of legislation and policies. With panelists from ILO, OHCHR, and representatives of workers in informal economy. We encourage all delegations to actively participate in the panel discussion and share their experiences and best practices. Thank you.

Thank you. The annual debate on the rights of persons with disabilities to be held under resolutions 7/9, 55/8 and 57.6 of the Council will be based on the topic "Rights of persons with disabilities digital technologies and assistance technologies, combating cyberbullying and digital inclusivity. This will be accessible to persons with disabilities. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Mexico to present this initiative on behalf of the main sponsors.

Thank you, President. I have the honour to make this statement on behalf of Mexico and New Zealand. Under resolution 55/8, adopted by the Human Rights Council on 3 April 2024, during the 58th session of the Council, there will be an interactive debate on the rights of persons with disabilities based on their rights and the technologies and tools available digitally, including support technologies. As part of the joint efforts to improve the Council's efficiency, Mexico and New Zealand have agreed with the members of the core group under resolution 51/10 on combating cyberbullying, led by Argentina, to hold an interactive joint debate addressing also combating of cyberbullying of persons with disabilities. We thank those delegations and the secretariat for their readiness and flexibility to organize the joint panel. The interactive dialogue will be held on Monday 10th March in this room during the afternoon and will have a format that is accessible to persons with disabilities. It will explore the role of digital technologies and assistance tools as key elements in systems for care and support and review how they are essential to guaranteeing the rights of persons with disabilities to live independently in their communities with dignity and in autonomy. It will also address challenges related to cyberbullying, privacy, access to information and informed decision-making. It will discuss how governance and digital technologies, when co-designed with persons with disabilities, can improve autonomy, social and political participation, access to services, can reduce administrative costs and reduce work involved in care and support, which disproportionately affects women. It will be moderated by Heba Hegras, Special Rapporteur on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, and with the participation of the following panellists: Sanha Tarchai, President of the Global Federation of Deaf and Blind Persons; Praveena Sukhesh Eeli, Director of Governance and Compliance of the Division of the Rights of Persons with Disabilities of the National Department for Women, Youth and Persons with Disabilities of South Africa. Digital creator and TV presenter with a focus on cyberbullying, the rights of persons with disabilities and health. We call on all delegations to participate in this annual interactive debate to share their points of view and their experience on this important topic. Thank you, President.

Thank you. The annual day on the rights of the child, to be held under resolution 7/29 and 55.29 of the Council, has the topic development of early childhood. and will also be available to persons with disabilities. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Uruguay to present this initiative on behalf of the main stakeholders.

Thank you, President. Representing the EU and members of CREW, we represent the annual Day on the Rights of the Child. organised by the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights under the resolution on the rights of the child and co-led by the European Union and the Group of European States of the Council of Europe. It will be held on 13 March, based on the development of early childhood, and will have two discussion panels. The first will analyse priorities in promoting focus on the development of the child, and the second on early childhood development in situations of emergency, giving priority to the rights of the child. More detail can be found in the concept note that is available on the intranet of the Human Rights Council.

The international day for the elimination of racial discrimination held under resolution 79161 of the General Assembly will be based on the topic 60th anniversary of the adoption of the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Ghana to present the initiative on behalf of the main sponsors.

Thank you, Mr. President. The African Group welcomes the convening of a panel discussion on the commemoration of the International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination to be held on 27 March 2025 during the Human Rights Council 58th session. It is gratifying to note that the panel discussion will focus on how to enhance implementation by states of the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination. It is the expectation of the African Group that the panel discussion will yield concrete outcomes, especially increase the capacity of all stakeholders to develop comprehensive and sustainable solutions to achieve racial justice and equality. We invite all Council members and observer states to prioritize this panel discussion by participating actively. I thank you very much.

Thank you. That brings us to the end of the updates on panels, and I encourage all participants to consult the concept notes on the extranet of the Council in the next few days. Excellencies, distinguished colleagues, We will now move to review of the programme of work. On 3 March, Monday, the Council will hear an oral update from the High Commissioner for Human Rights. The general debate on the oral update will be held following the presentation by the High Commissioner of several country-specific reports and mandated updates under item 2 of the agenda. During the session, the Council will hold 31 interactive dialogues with the High Commissioner, the Bureau and the designated experts, special procedures mandate holders and mandate holders of the investigation mechanisms and the special representatives of the Secretary-General. The Council will also hold five extended interactive debates, one high-level debate and nine general debates. The Council will also adopt the results of the UPR for Norway, Albania, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Cote d'Ivoire, Portugal, Bhutan, Dominica, the DPRK, Brunei, Darussalam, Costa Rica, Equatorial Guinea, Ethiopia, Qatar and Nicaragua examined at the 48th session of the Working Group on the Universal Periodic Review. Excellencies, distinguished participants, towards the end of the session, the Council will proceed to select three mandate holders for expert mechanisms. My list of proposed candidates will be disseminated and published on the extranet. I take this opportunity to thank the members of the advisory group for their work. I recall that on 10 January this year, the Bureau examined the question of the representative of the Union of Myanmar. within the Human Rights Council and noted that the situation remained unchanged since 2021. In keeping with the practice of the past four years, the bureau took note of the fact that the situation relating to the representation of Myanmar in the Human Rights Council remained unchanged. Consequently, it was noted that, pending the decision of the General Assembly on this matter, the secretariat of the Human Rights Council could not address requests for participation by anybody belonging to the delegation of Myanmar within the Council in 2025. In keeping with the previous decisions of the Council, the Bureau proposed to the Council that the two interactive dialogues planned at the 58th session on Myanmar, namely the interactive dialogue on the oral update of the High Commissioner concerning Myanmar And the interactive dialogue with the Special Rapporteur on the human rights situation in Myanmar should be held as planned, without participation by the concerned country. This is proposed on the basis that this exceptional circumstance does not constitute a precedent for the future. Do any members of the Council wish to comment on this proposal?

I understand that there is no objection to the Bureau's proposal to proceed with the two interactive dialogues on Myanmar as planned without the participation of the country concerned. It is so decided. Excellencies, distinguished colleagues, are there any delegations wishing to take the floor at this stage to comment on the draft programme of work as it is currently presented? Please note that we'll discuss the modalities for the 58th session and share information on draft resolutions and other initiatives by delegations at a later stage of this meeting. I don't see any requests from the floor. Excellencies, distinguished colleagues, the deadline for submitting draft proposals for the 58th session will be Thursday, 21 March, at 13:00. Any request for an extension will only be approved by the Commission in exceptional circumstances for a maximum of 24 hours by the Council. In this context, let me kindly ask all delegations to submit their draft proposals on time. The e-delegate gate platform will continue to be used for the submission and sponsorship of draft resolutions, and states are encouraged to check in advance that they have access to e-delegate. The three-year program of work for 2025-2027 was last updated on 3 January 2025 and was published on the extranet. Let me remind the main sponsors of draft resolutions that they are encouraged to take into account the multi-year program of work when proposing new initiatives. I now request delegations to share information on draft resolutions and other initiatives. Delegations wishing to speak in the room should raise their nameplates. Are there any requests for the floor? Oh, I see quite a few. Algeria first. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Algeria.

Thank you, President. At the outset, I'd like to express my congratulations on your election to guide the work of the Council, and rest assured of the support of my delegation to ensure success of your mandate. On the occasion of the 58th session, Algeria will be presenting, as part of the core group, including South Africa, Croatia, Mozambique, the United Kingdom, Peru, and Vanuatu, a draft resolution on the impact of anti-personnel mines on the enjoyment of human rights. This initiative aims at focusing on the impact of the use of anti-personnel mines on human rights and fundamental freedoms. Anti-personnel mines affect principally civilians, especially in post-conflict war zones, that they lead to serious injuries and permanent disabilities, and they deprive local communities of access to essential resources like land, water, and basic infrastructure. That is a violation of the right to life, security, and human dignity. On behalf of the Core Group, Algeria invites all countries to participate in negotiations in a constructive manner and will work towards making sure that this resolution is adopted on the day that will be associated with the celebration of the International Day in line with the resolution of the UN General Assembly. Now, the Human Rights Council, the ICRC, and the International Campaign to Ban Anti-Personnel Landmines, Algeria will be organizing a parallel event on the theme of the resolution. This event will take place on 11 March. 2025 from 11 to 1 p.m. with the participation of panelists, especially Special Rapporteur on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. The objective is to assess the impact of anti-personal mines on human rights during and after conflicts. My delegation hopes to see many of you participate in that roundtable. Thank you.
Next one is Pakistan, followed by the Netherlands, Mexico, Cuba, and Spain. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Pakistan.

Thank you, Mr. President. The OIC congratulates you on assuming the HRC presidency and assures you of our cooperation in the discharge of your important responsibilities. The upcoming session of the Council will be held under a challenging global human rights landscape. We are confident that under your leadership, the Council will focus its efforts and respond constructively and collaboratively. During the forthcoming session, the OIC group intends to present the following traditional resolutions under items 2 and 7 of the Council's agenda, which form part of the international community's normative response to the continuous tragedy in the Middle East. Number one, human rights situation in the occupied Palestinian territory, including East Jerusalem, and the obligation to ensure accountability and justice. Number two, right of the Palestinian people to self-determination. Number three, Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territory, including East Jerusalem and the occupied Syrian Golan. And number four, human rights in the occupied Syrian Golan. The group intends also to introduce the resolution on combating intolerance, negative stereotyping and stigmatization of and discrimination, incitement to violence and violence against persons based on religion or belief under item 9. At a time of sharply increasing discrimination, incitement and violence based on religion, especially Islamophobia, the resolution represents the bare minimum and we hope to see its consensual adoption translated into tangible action. As in the past, we expect the Council to lend its full support to the Group's draft resolutions and assures you, likewise, of our constructive engagement. Thank you, sir.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Kingdom of the Netherlands.

Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you. Thank you for allowing me to invite, with sincere pleasure, all delegations and civil society colleagues to attend the high-level event How to protect journalists and civilians' right to access to information in times of conflict. This will be hosted by the Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, His Excellency Casper Veldkamp, on Wednesday, the 26th of February, from 9 to 10 in Room 24. And this high-level event will showcase the power of journalism in conflict settings and demonstrates how journalists and other media workers function as a lifeline for civilians. It will further underscore the obligations and responsibilities of states to protect journalists in conflict settings. The event will feature testimonies from journalists working in conflict settings, including Sudan, Ukraine and Gaza, and bring together state representatives, UN officials and civil society with the aim of strengthening and renewing our common commitment towards the safety of journalists. And I hope to see many of you at that event, and I thank you, Mr. President.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Mexico.

Thank you very much, President. I'm pleased to inform you that during the 50th session, Mexico will be presenting a draft resolution related to the mandate of the Special Rapporteur on the promotion and protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms in the fight against terrorism. This draft resolution of a procedural nature, has as its objective to renew the mandate of the Special Rapporteur for a period of three additional years. Mr. President, in 2025, we'll be celebrating 20 years since the establishment of the mandate of the Special Rapporteur that was created on the basis of Resolution 2005/80 of the Human Rights Commission, presented by Mexico and adopted on the 21st of April, 2005. The last renewal of the mandate was done based on resolution 49/10 of this Council, adopted by consensus on the 31st of March 2022, with 60 countries co-sponsoring the resolution. We thank all the delegations that supported the mandate throughout its history and invite the Council to renew the mandate once again. Also, just like every year, Mexico, together with Finland, will be presenting a joint statement to commemorate the International Women's Day. We do hope to receive support of other delegations. Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Cuba.

Thank you, President. Good afternoon. The delegation of Cuba would like to reiterate our support to your work and wish you full success to you and members of the Bureau as you carry out your functions. We welcome the new members of the Council, and we ensure them of the willingness of Cuba to work with all of them in a constructive and cooperative manner. We live in an international context that is even more complex since 20th of January, characterized by serious threats to the UN Charter, international law, the President of the United States, seems to be interpreting his arrival to power as a position of an emperor, showing disrespect to the international cooperation, multilateral institutions, announcing that the country will be withdrawing from the Human Rights Council, the WHO, and the Paris Agreement. This government's ambitions include the conquest of Canada, the occupation of Greenland, the change of name to the Gulf of Mexico, and taking the Panama Canal away from Panamanians, violating the rights of regular migrants in the country that's suffering from indiscriminate deportations. The discriminatory policy against Cuba has become unprecedented, leading to flagrant violations of the human rights of Cuban people. The Human Rights Council cannot remain impassive facing these realities. that require our attention and actions. In these circumstances, we call upon all members to renew their commitment to the mandate of this body. Mr. President, in the upcoming session of the Council, Cuba will be presenting three draft resolutions in its national capacity: the draft on the right to Food will relate to the renewal of the mandate of the Special Rapporteur, whose work helped deal with food insecurity, hunger, and extreme poverty, and provide support to developing countries in the production of agricultural products, imports, strengthening food, sustainable food systems, and productive development of national industry. We also will be submitting a draft resolution on the consequences of foreign debt and other related financial international obligations of states and the full enjoyment of human rights, especially economic, social, and cultural rights. That text has as its objectives to ensure that the impact of foreign debt remains visual, the impact on human rights, including the right to development. And also, it'll focus on the urgent need to reform the unjust and anti-democratic international financial system. Finally, the draft resolution on the promotion of the enjoyment of cultural rights of all and respect for cultural diversity will highlight the importance to respect national specific features, as well as historic, cultural, and religious diversities between and among states. that develop their own economic and social systems. In conclusion, I would say that the Cuban delegation is ready to work in a constructive, transparent, and inclusive manner with all delegations and civil society organizations in informal consultations and other platforms as we negotiate these three proposals. And we thank in advance the support of all of you. Thank you.

Thank you. Colleagues, I'd like to remind you that this is an organizational meeting, and I would like to invite you to respect the nature of this meeting and to concentrate exclusively on the presentation of your initiatives at this stage. Thank you very much. Spain is next on my list, followed by Bolivia, Cyprus, Colombia, Ghana, and Iceland. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Spain.

Thank you, President. committed to the recognition of the rights of caretakers and that provide support. This will provide the opportunity to share experiences and best practices that relate to the promotion and respect of human rights of those who provide care and those who are cared. And in order to ensure sustainable development. Also, Spain, as the distinguished delegate of Morocco will speak at a later stage, we're part of a group of countries that have been promoting a resolution related to the role of women in diplomacy, promoting gender equality in multilateralism as a fundamental element to ensure peace and security, sustainable development, and human rights of everyone. Thank you.
I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Bolivia.

This event will take place on the 7th of March, Friday. at 1 p.m. in room 24. Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Cyprus.

Thank you, Mr. President. On behalf of a cross-regional core group comprised of Argentina, Ethiopia, Greece, Iraq, Ireland, Italy, Mali, Poland, and Serbia, and my own country, Cyprus, I wish to inform you that we will be presenting the triennial resolution on cultural rights and the protection of cultural heritage under agenda item three of the session. The HRC plays a vital role in calling upon all states to respect, promote, and protect the right of everyone to take part in cultural life, including the ability to access and enjoy cultural heritage. The draft will be updated to reflect developments since its previous iteration, while maintaining its human-based rights approach to cultural heritage protection. The zero draft will be circulated as we get closer to the session and we look forward to engaging with you with a view to its consensual adoption. Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Colombia. Gracias.

Thank you. Thank you, President. Colombia would like to congratulate you on your election as President. We wish you full success. On basis of our experience during previous decades, during this session, 58th session, the Human Rights Council will be hosting a parallel event with the participation of the Special Rapporteur on the Protection of Human Rights Defenders as part of her preparation of the future report on human rights defenders in rural areas and other contexts. Two human rights defenders will participate in this work, and they will share their experience, challenges, and achievements in the protection of human rights in different parts of the world. We do hope you can participate in this event. We also will be hosting an event together with the Dominican Republic on mechanisms related to implementation and follow-up to international recommendations, and an event on sexual and reproductive health organized with other states and not governmental organizations. Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Ghana.

Thank you, Mr. President. I am pleased to inform that the African group will present three resolutions during the upcoming 58th session, as follows. Under agenda item 3, the group will present for consideration the biennial resolution on the negative impact of the non-repatriation of funds of illicit origin on the enjoyment of human rights. Two, under agenda item 10, a resolution in respect of the mandate renewal for the technical assistance and capacity building for Mali in the field of human rights. Thank you, Mr. President. On behalf of Germany, Moldova, North Macedonia, United Kingdom, and my own country, Iceland, I would like to inform the Council that we will present a resolution on the situation of human rights in the Islamic Republic of Iran. We will hold open and formal consultations in line with standard Council practice, and we look forward to engaging with colleagues on this important resolution in the weeks ahead. We welcome the continued engagement with the South Sudanese Government with the Commission and note the progress that has been made. However, further work is needed to support the recently extended revitalized peace agreement, including to continue to collect evidence on human rights violations to contribute to accountability, transitional justice and long-term peace. Secondly, Mr. President, we have all seen the historic developments in Syria in recent months. With the fall of the Assad regime, the revelations of the horrors faced by the Syrian people have been laid bare. Their aspirations for a future Syria grounded in human rights, freedom, and justice deserve this Council's full support. We welcome the engagement between the Interim Authorities and OHCHR, the Commission of Inquiry, and the International Impartial and Independent Mechanism, and the Independent Institution on Missing Persons. We very much hope that such positive engagement continues in order to facilitate an eventual Syrian-led transitional justice process. So the UK, as part of a core group, will therefore present a resolution renewing the mandate of the Commission of Inquiry to ensure that its vital work in documenting violations and abuses in Syria can continue. Indeed, we hope that its work will be enhanced by sustained access which they have until now been denied. In doing so, we look to support crucial efforts to hold those responsible for violations and abuses to account and contribute to the process of reconciliation and healing. We will hold open informal negotiations on both resolutions in line with standard Council practice. Thank you.

Human rights are the same and apply in the same manner online and offline. Thank you, President. We're happy to see you presiding over the Human Rights Council. And we reiterate our full support to you.

This anniversary of Russia's military aggression against Ukraine and three years since its full-scale invasion, the devastating impact of this war on human rights and fundamental freedoms is impossible to overstate. At the upcoming session, Ukraine will continue to draw the Council's attention to the ongoing crimes committed by Russia, stressing the urgent need for justice and accountability. Russia's daily deliberate attacks on civilian and critical infrastructure and residential areas, execution and inhumane treatment of prisoners of war and civilian detainees, unlawful deportation and forcible transfer of Ukrainian children. These crimes require a resolute global response. Ensuring justice for all victims of this war of aggression is a top priority. for Ukraine, we will continue working to hold Russia accountable for its crimes and to support all mechanisms that document and investigate these violations. In this regard, we will introduce an updated resolution on the human rights situation in Ukraine, extending the mandate of the Independent International Commission of Inquiry for another year. This commission plays a critical role in gathering evidence that will serve as a foundation for accountability in future international legal proceedings. We count on the strong support of Human Rights Council member states for this initiative and call for constructive engagement in the interactive dialogue following the presentation of reports by the Commission of Inquiry and the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights. At the same time, Ukraine remains fully committed to the broader human rights agenda and stands ready for an open and meaningful dialogue on all pressing human rights issues. The international community must stand firm in defending human rights and upholding justice. Failure to act will be a betrayal of the very principles of justice and humanity that bind us all. In this regard, I wish to underline an intrinsic link between Geneva and New York, peace and human rights, and call upon the countries represented in this room to support the draft UN General Assembly resolution calling for advancement of a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace for Ukraine. I thank you.

We remain concerned about the human rights situation in Belarus. with repression of independent and dissenting voices, arbitrary detentions, widespread torture, the denial of due process and the right to a fair trial, and systematic impunity. Secondly, we will present, together with Australia, the resolution on the Democratic People's Republic of Korea. This situation continues to draw attention to the human rights and humanitarian issues in the DPRK, and we will express continued support for the work on accountability and the need to address the findings of the Commission of Inquiry from 2014. Finally, the EU will also present again a resolution on freedom of religion or belief in order to underline the Council's commitment to the promotion and protection of the right to freedom of religion or belief. All human beings, wherever they live, should be guaranteed the right to have or not to have, to choose, change or leave, to practice and to manifest their religion or belief without fear of violence, persecution or discrimination. For all these resolutions, we look forward to working constructively with colleagues and partners in the informal consultations, as well as on other initiatives. Thank you, President.

Thank you, President. On behalf of a cross-regional core group consisting of Chile, Singapore, Switzerland, and Greece, I would like to announce that the resolution on neurotechnology and human rights will be presented during the upcoming HRC session. The neurotechnology and human rights resolution was first adopted by consensus at the 51st session of the Council with a wide range of co-sponsors. The resolution focused on the impact, opportunities, and challenges of neurotechnology with regard to the promotion and protection of all human rights and mandated the Advisory Committee of the Human Rights Council to draft a report on the outcomes of its study on this topic. The report was presented to the Council at its 57th session. Neurotechnology is at the cutting edge of scientific and technological innovation, offering unprecedented possibilities in fields as wide-ranging as healthcare, communication, accessibility, and cognitive enhancement. It has the potential to significantly improve human well-being and promote human rights, particularly by advancing medical treatments for neurological disorders, enhancing the lives of individuals with disabilities, and enabling new forms of human-computer interaction. As neurotechnology evolves rapidly, we also need to be alert to the ethical, legal, and societal concerns associated with its use. The ability to assess, manipulate, or influence brain activity and mental processes raises complex questions that need answers consistent with human rights. Therefore, it is imperative to raise awareness and ensure that neurotechnology serves humanity in a responsible manner. With this resolution, we aim to engage in a constructive discussion and continued collaboration on this crucial issue. In this context, the core group also plans to organize a side event aiming to foster awareness and to contribute to the multidisciplinary dialogue on the opportunities and challenges of neurotechnology and human rights. The zero draft of the resolution will be circulated in due course. We look forward to engaging with all of you on this important topic. Thank you.

In the upcoming HRC 58, Portugal will once again present the traditional omnibus resolution on the question of the realization in all countries of economic, social and cultural rights. This is a 30-year-old consensual resolution which dates back to the Human Rights Commission, gathering support from all regional groups. For years, Portugal has been one of the main advocates of economic, social and cultural rights. Back in the day, the idea of the existence of a hierarchy of rights still prevailed, a misconception that time came to demystify. Today we are happy to see that there is a broad consensus on the understanding that economic, social and cultural must be treated in a fair and equal manner, on the same footing and with the same emphasis as civil and political rights, as enshrined in the Vienna Declaration and Programme of Action. However, much remains to be done globally for the fulfillment of economic, social, and cultural rights. At this critical juncture, our commitment remains strong. Portugal will continue its leadership on this matter, defending the universal, indivisible, interrelated, interdependent, and mutually reinforcing nature of all human rights. This year's resolution will specifically address the topic of financing for development. We count on your constructive engagement during negotiations. Thank you.

I thank delegations for sharing information on their initiatives. Let me emphasize that under resolution 5/1, delegations are invited to conduct informal consultations of an open nature in order to ensure the widest possible support of their initiatives. At least one open-ended informal consultation should take place on each draft resolution and/or decision before it is submitted to the Council for consideration. Consultations should, to the extent possible, be timely, transparent and inclusive, taking into account the constraints faced by delegations, especially smaller ones. This will help to create a constructive working atmosphere based on transparency, dialogue, and cooperation. Excellencies, distinguished Colleagues, let us continue with the modalities of the session. For the meetings of the 58th session of the Human Rights Council, States and other observers, NGOs in consultative status with ECOSOC, as well as national human rights institutions with A status, will have the opportunity to present their statements in person or through pre-recorded video statements. In order to reconcile the importance of inclusiveness with what is achievable in terms of time and resources, the list of speakers for NGOs during each general debate will be based on the average number of NGOs that participated in each general debate during the previous three March sessions. In other words, 50. 52nd and 49th sessions. With regard to the working hours of the session, I wish to recall that on 10 January, I informed the Bureau that I received a letter from the Prime Minister of Pakistan on behalf of the OIC, requesting that the working hours of the 58th session during Ramadan be adjusted in the same manner as at the 55th session in March last year. namely, the meetings are held from 9:30 a.m. 30 p.m. and from 2:30 to 5:30 p.m. I then conducted additional consultations, including with the Director General of UNOCH, who confirmed that such an adjustment could be taken into account by UNOCH if the Council decides to pursue that option. also consulted regional groups through their coordinators, and no objections have been recorded.
